sentences.text: Geosaurus is an extinct marine crocodyliform belonging to the Crurotarsi group, the evolutionary lineage that leads to modern crocodilians.
The type species, Geosaurus giganteus, meaning 'giant land lizard', reached lengths of about 2.5 to 3 meters.
Fossil evidence for this species includes a complete skull.
Another species, Geosaurus lapparenti, is known from the Early Cretaceous period in south-east France.
A large, undescribed species is known from a single tooth found in the Plattenkalk of Germany.
The modern Chinese name for this animal is Dilong, which translates to 'earth dragon'.
The type species was discovered in Late Jurassic deposits located in Western Europe, specifically Germany.
The genus was established by Georges Cuvier in 1824.
It was originally named Lacerta gigantea by von Sömmerring before being reclassified.
Geosaurus grandis, described by Wagner in 1858, was formerly considered a species of Cricosaurus.
Geosaurus lapparenti was originally classified as a species of Dakosaurus.
Geosaurus carpenteri, also referred to as Dakosaurus at the time, is known from a partial skull.
Geosaurus was a carnivore that likely spent its entire life in the ocean.
Geosaurus giganteus and Dakosaurus maximus were likely the top predators in their ecosystem, characterized by large size, short snouts, and serrated teeth.

Dakosaurus and G. giganteus appear to have been the main predators in this area, possessing large serrated teeth in a short-snouted skull, contrasting with Cricosaurus and Rhacheosaurus, both equipped with long, thin snouts specialized for fish and other small prey.
Researchers hypothesize that niche partitioning allowed multiple species of crocodyliforms to coexist in the same environment.
Alongside Dakosaurus maximus, three species of Geosaurus are known from the Mörnsheim Formation in Bavaria, Germany.
No eggs or nests of Geosaurus have been found, leaving its lifecycle largely unknown.
A revised classification presented by Young and Andrade in 2009 was used to list valid species after they published a redescription examining relationships.

They found that several species previously classified in Geosaurus, including G. suevicus, G. saltillense, G. vignaudi, and G. araucanensis, were actually species of the closely related genus Cricosaurus.
Rhacheosaurus gracilis, another long-snouted species, was also considered a species of Geosaurus (G. gracilis).
The genus belongs to the family Metriorhynchidae and its parent group is Geosaurina, placing it within the class Reptilia.
Geosaurus lived from the Late Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous periods, with a time range from the Oxfordian to the Hauterivian (159 to 125.77 million years ago).
There are 17 recorded fossil occurrences of this genus.
Phylogenetic analyses starting in 2005 suggested that the genus Geosaurus is not monophyletic, and these analyses did not support Geosaurus as a monophyletic group.
